whyCorrect: Read the sentence the word sits in: the mesh does something "as the load comes on," and the result is that the force stays lower than a rigid surface would produce. The net is physically deflecting under weight instead of resisting it. "Gives way" is exactly that physical sense of stretching or moving under a load.

whyWrong.A: "Concedes a point" is the argument sense of the word, and nothing here is a debate — the subject is a mesh under a falling worker.
whyWrong.C: "Surrenders" implies giving up in a contest, and it also suggests total failure; the net does not fail, it deflects and keeps working.
whyWrong.D: "Produces" is a real meaning of the word, but it needs an object that gets made, and the sentence names no product — the mesh yields, it does not yield something.

commonMistakes: Choosing a dictionary meaning the word really has, without checking which meaning the grammar of this sentence allows.
tips: When a word has several common senses, let the surrounding physical situation pick one.

whyCorrect: The whole passage contrasts what can be dated with what cannot: charcoal carries carbon from a living tree, so it can be dated directly, while ochre is mineral and its age is the rock's age, not the artist's. The blank must name the property the two techniques do not share equally, and that property is being able to be dated.

whyWrong.B: Durability is never discussed — the passage says nothing about which pigment lasts longer on the wall.
whyWrong.C: Visibility is irrelevant; both kinds of figures are visible, which is why they can be compared at all.
whyWrong.D: Elaborateness concerns how detailed a drawing is, and the passage compares dating methods, not artistic complexity.

tips: The blank in a Words in Context item is usually a one-word summary of the contrast the passage just drew.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank gives a cause-and-effect: runny basaltic lava spreads into sheets, stiffer lava piles up into a mound. Different chemistry yields different shapes, so the chemistry sets the shape. "Determined" states that causal relationship.

whyWrong.A: "Borrowed" would mean the shape was taken from somewhere else, and the passage names no source to borrow from.
whyWrong.C: "Obscured" means hidden, which contradicts the passage — the chemistry reveals why the shape is what it is, not conceals it.
whyWrong.D: "Reversed" would mean the chemistry undoes the shape, but nothing in the text describes a shape being turned around or undone.

tips: When a passage gives two parallel examples of cause producing effect, the blank almost always names causation.

whyCorrect: Each grade of cloth is described as good for one condition and bad for another: heavy cloth holds shape in a gale but is stiff in light air, light cloth draws well in a breeze but stretches when pressed. The final sentence contrasts the exercise with "finding a single best cloth," so the blank must name accepting a trade-off. That is compromise.

whyWrong.A: "Improvisation" means making it up as you go, but the loft stocks graded cloths in advance and chooses deliberately.
whyWrong.C: "Duplication" means making copies, and nothing is being copied.
whyWrong.D: "Concealment" means hiding something, which has no basis anywhere in the passage.

commonMistakes: Skipping the phrase "rather than in finding a single best cloth," which is the clue that no option is fully right.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts Braille's six-dot cell, which a fingertip reads at rest, with earlier alphabets that copied printed shapes the finger had to trace. The closing phrase "rather than to the eye" tells you the blank describes a good match to touch. "Suited" is that match.

whyWrong.B: "Opposed" reverses the logic — the design works with the sense of touch, not against it.
whyWrong.C: "Invisible" describes the eye, but the sentence's contrast puts the blank on the side of touch, and invisibility is not why the design succeeded.
whyWrong.D: "Indifferent" would mean the design ignored touch, the opposite of the reason the passage gives for its success.

tips: The word after the blank — here "to" — narrows the options; "suited to" and "opposed to" both fit grammatically, so the meaning of the contrast decides it.

whyCorrect: The text opens by saying two figures on one wall need not share an age, then explains why a gap leaves no trace, then draws its own conclusion: date each datable mark and admit the rest float free, "rather than assigning a single date to the chamber." That final clause is the main idea, stated by the passage itself.

whyWrong.B: This is the position the passage argues against — it says a wall may be painted, left a thousand years, and painted again.
whyWrong.C: The passage never claims radiocarbon is the only method; it only says some marks can be dated and others cannot.
whyWrong.D: Nothing says early images are lost; repainting is offered as a reason dates differ, not as a cause of destruction.

commonMistakes: Picking an option that repeats a detail from the middle of the passage instead of the conclusion the passage builds toward.

whyCorrect: Every sentence describes one process: flat cloths are cut with a curved edge, sewn together, and the result bellies out into a three-dimensional shape. The last sentence adds how the curve is measured and laid off. The purpose is to explain that procedure.

whyWrong.B: No comparison of hand cutting with machine cutting appears, so there is no argument for one being better.
whyWrong.C: The loft floor is mentioned only as the surface the curve is marked on — the building's history is never traced.
whyWrong.D: Weather is not the topic; the passage describes making one sail's shape, not matching sails to conditions.

tips: For "main purpose," ask what the text does — explain, argue, compare, trace — and check that the verb matches every sentence, not just one.

whyCorrect: The first sentence concedes strength but explicitly rejects it as the reason ("that is not why it is used"). The rest of the passage gives the real reason: a bar takes a permanent set or cracks when bent, while a rope's thin wires slide against one another and can be wound thousands of times. Repeated bending without damage is the stated cause.

whyWrong.A: Ease of manufacture is never mentioned; the explanation is about bending behaviour, not production.
whyWrong.C: The passage compares a rope with a bar of the same weight, not the same dimensions, and it sets that strength claim aside as not the point.
whyWrong.D: The drum is what forces the bending, not something designed to reduce it — the rope adapts to the drum, not the reverse.

commonMistakes: Choosing the strength claim in the opening sentence, which the same sentence immediately rules out as the reason.

whyCorrect: The passage gives the chain explicitly: the thread passes round cords laid across the spine, the cords are laced into the boards, and so "the covers are attached to the sewing rather than to the paper." Because nothing joins the covers to the leaves directly, removing the covers leaves the leaves untouched.

whyWrong.A: Trimming is never mentioned, and trimming would cut the leaves rather than protect them.
whyWrong.B: The text says the opposite — the thread passes through the fold of each gathering.
whyWrong.D: Glue along the spine is exactly what the described binding avoids; a glued spine is what would make the leaves impossible to separate from the cover.

tips: An "according to the text" question is answered by a sentence you can point at, not by what sounds plausible about bookbinding.

whyCorrect: Vollan's claim is comparative: diameter matters more than the number of bends. Supporting it needs both quantities set against each other. Going from 10,000 to 40,000 bends costs at most 7 points (58 to 51, 89 to 85, 96 to 94), while at 10,000 bends changing the sheave from 30× to 10× costs 96 − 58 = 38 points. The larger effect belongs to diameter, which is the argument.

whyWrong.A: A single figure from one row shows a large sheave preserves strength, but with nothing to compare it to it says nothing about which factor matters more.
whyWrong.B: That all ropes lost some strength with more bends supports the factor Vollan says matters less, and it ignores diameter entirely.
whyWrong.D: This reports only the smallest-sheave row. Both numbers come from the same diameter, so the comparison it makes is between bend counts, not between diameters.

commonMistakes: Picking a true statement from the table that does not compare the two variables the argument compares.

whyCorrect: Halloran claims layout matters more than cloth grade. A finding supports that only if it varies each factor while holding the other fixed. Choice A does exactly that: same cloth, different layouts gives a big difference; same layout, different grades gives almost none. That isolates layout as the driver.

whyWrong.B: This is about cloth grade alone under a fixed load; it says nothing about layout, and if anything it points to the factor Halloran downplays.
whyWrong.C: Speed of manufacture has nothing to do with whether a sail keeps its shape.
whyWrong.D: Disagreement among sailmakers is an opinion, not evidence about what actually happens to a sail after a season.

tips: For a "which finding would support" item, look for the option that controls one variable while changing the other.

whyCorrect: "Speed alone" is a claim with two halves: contracted braille is faster, and it is not better on anything else measured. You need data on both columns. Choice D gives the speed gap (118 against 74) and the near-identical comprehension scores (82 percent against 81), which together show the advantage does not extend beyond speed.

whyWrong.A: This proves the speed half only. It leaves open the possibility that contracted braille also improves comprehension, which would refute "alone."
whyWrong.B: This proves the comprehension half only, and by itself it makes contracted braille look no better at anything.
whyWrong.C: This describes how the study was run rather than reporting any result, so it cannot support a claim about the outcome.

commonMistakes: Treating the word "alone" as decoration; it is what forces you to use both columns of the table.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up a cause and its consequence: cloth that creeps lengthens under sustained load, and a sail that lengthens no longer shows the curve it was cut to. Laminates are then said to hold their length. Follow the chain — no lengthening means the designed curve survives — and the conclusion is that a laminate sail keeps its shape longer.

whyWrong.A: Repair is never discussed, and a bonded laminate offers no stated reason to be easier to mend.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the point: the laminate's virtue is that it stretches less, and breaking load is a different property from creep.
whyWrong.D: Weight is not compared anywhere; the passage's contrast is about holding length, not mass.

tips: When a blank follows "therefore," the answer is the endpoint of the causal chain the passage just laid out — not a new fact about the subject.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the rule: a system reproduces the distribution of its training text. The second says the parliamentary corpus is heavy on formal argument and light on kitchen and playground language. Applying the rule to that corpus, the system inherits the imbalance and performs better on the register it saw most.

whyWrong.A: Equal facility between any two languages contradicts the stated rule that output follows the training data, and the passage discusses register, not language pairs.
whyWrong.B: Sentence length is never mentioned, and reproducing the training distribution would suggest similar lengths, not shorter ones.
whyWrong.C: The passage gives no mechanism for improvement without new training; it describes what the training data fixes in place.

commonMistakes: Inferring something about machine translation in general instead of the one consequence this passage's premises force.

whyCorrect: "The building's single purpose is written into its proportions" and "nothing else needs a room that shape" are both complete sentences, and the second explains the first. A colon is the mark for introducing an explanation after a complete clause, so it joins them correctly.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation at all the two complete sentences run together into a fused sentence.
whyWrong.B: Adding "and" plus a pair of commas cuts "nothing" off from its own verb, leaving "else needs a room" without a subject.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two complete sentences is a comma splice; a comma cannot do the work of a colon or a period here.

tips: Test each side of the punctuation on its own — if both sides stand alone as sentences, a comma is never enough.

whyCorrect: "The load a fibre bundle can carry depends on how the load is shared out among its members" and "the sharing depends in turn on how tightly the bundle is twisted" are both independent clauses, and they are joined by the coordinating conjunction and. The convention is a comma before a coordinating conjunction that links two independent clauses.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon joins two independent clauses by itself; adding "and" after it gives the sentence two connectors doing one job.
whyWrong.B: Leaving out the comma before "and" fails the rule for joining two independent clauses, since both sides here have their own subject and verb.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation or a list, but the second clause continues the point rather than spelling out the first.

commonMistakes: Assuming "and" never takes a comma; the test is whether what follows it could stand alone as a sentence.

whyCorrect: "The fungal threads that sheathe a root are thinner than the finest root hair" and "they reach into pores no root could enter" are each complete sentences, and so is a coordinating conjunction. Two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction take a comma before it.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon already joins two independent clauses on its own, so pairing it with "so" doubles the connector.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces an explanation or list and cannot be followed by a coordinating conjunction.
whyWrong.D: Dropping the comma leaves two independent clauses joined only by "so," which the convention does not allow.

tips: The seven coordinating conjunctions — for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — take a comma when what follows them could stand alone.

whyCorrect: "When a flow's crust thickens enough to bear a person's weight" begins with when, so it is a dependent clause, and it comes before the main clause. An introductory dependent clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the dependent clause runs straight into the main clause, so the reader cannot see where the condition ends.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon links two independent clauses, but the first part here cannot stand alone as a sentence.
whyWrong.D: A colon must follow a complete sentence, and "When a flow's crust thickens enough to bear a person's weight" is not one.

commonMistakes: Treating any long opening stretch of words as a full clause; a word like when, although, or because at the front makes it dependent.

whyCorrect: The clause after "so" has a subject — "its rendering of kitchen talk" — and no other verb, so the blank must be a finite verb. The first clause is in the past perfect ("had been trained"), which places the whole account in the past, so the simple past surprised is the form that fits.

whyWrong.A: "Surprising" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the second clause would be left with no predicate.
whyWrong.B: An infinitive cannot serve as the main verb of a clause; "its rendering to surprise nobody" is not a sentence.
whyWrong.D: "Surprise" does not agree with the singular subject "rendering" and it puts the sentence in the present while the rest is in the past.

tips: Find the subject of the clause first; if it has no verb yet, the blank has to be a finite one.

whyCorrect: "And then" joins the blank to the earlier verb laced, so the two verbs share the subject "the binder" and must match in form. The simple past covered is parallel with laced.

whyWrong.A: "Covers" is present tense and clashes with the past-tense "laced" in the same compound predicate.
whyWrong.B: "Covering" is a participle and breaks the parallel structure the conjunction sets up.
whyWrong.C: "Has covered" is present perfect, which pairs a completed-in-the-past action with a tense that connects to the present; the two joined verbs would no longer match.

tips: When two verbs share one subject across "and," the second copies the form of the first.

whyCorrect: The blank needs a possessive determiner in front of the noun "view," and the thing possessing the view is the plural "witnesses." Their is the plural possessive.

whyWrong.B: "There" is an adverb of place or an expletive subject; it cannot show possession of "view."
whyWrong.C: "They're" is the contraction of they are, which would give "they are view of the face."
whyWrong.D: "Its" is singular and would have to refer to one thing, but the owners of the view are the witnesses, who are plural.

commonMistakes: Choosing by sound — all three of their, there and they're sound alike, so decide by the job the word does in the sentence.

whyCorrect: The first sentence names one advantage of a lava tube — it shields the lava and slows heat loss. The second names a second, separate advantage: it keeps the flow narrow instead of letting it spread and thin. Two advantages stacked in the same direction call for an additive transition.

whyWrong.A: "Beforehand" claims a time sequence, but confining the flow is not something that happens earlier than the shielding.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" would require the second sentence to oppose the first, and both describe things that help the lava keep moving.
whyWrong.D: "For instance" would make the second sentence an example of the first, but confining a flow is not an instance of losing heat slowly.

tips: Ask whether the second sentence agrees with, opposes, or illustrates the first before you look at the options.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says heavier cloth is better at holding shape, which sets you up to expect the heaviest grade to be the best choice. The second sentence blocks that expectation: the heaviest grade will not set well in light air. A contrast transition marks that reversal.

whyWrong.B: "Therefore" would mean the second sentence follows from the first, but the first would predict the opposite conclusion.
whyWrong.C: "Similarly" signals two like cases, and these two statements pull against each other.
whyWrong.D: "In addition" adds a further point in the same direction, and the second sentence goes the other way.

commonMistakes: Reading only the first sentence and reaching for "therefore" because the topic feels like cause and effect.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim about where wire rope is used — wherever a load turns round a drum or sheave. The second names one specific piece of machinery and counts its bends. Moving from a general rule to one case calls for an illustrative transition.

whyWrong.A: "Even so" concedes something and then pushes back, but the crane example agrees with the general claim rather than resisting it.
whyWrong.C: "In contrast" needs an opposition, and the crane is a straightforward instance of the rule.
whyWrong.D: "As a result" would make the crane's design a consequence of the general statement, but the sentence reports an example, not an effect.

tips: A sentence that names one specific case right after a general statement is almost always signalled by "for example."

whyCorrect: The goal is the limits of invariants, so the answer has to carry the negative notes: matching values do not prove two knots are the same, and no known invariant separates every pair. Choice D states both, and it keeps the one thing invariants do prove as the contrast that makes the limit clear.

whyWrong.A: This gives only the definition and the deformation property — all capability, no limit.
whyWrong.B: This states what invariants successfully prove and adds a second positive property; nothing here is a limitation.
whyWrong.C: This does name one limit, but it drops the more important one — that equal values leave the question open — and pairs it with a bare definition.

tips: Match the goal's key word ("limits") to the notes that are negative, then choose the option that uses the most of them.

whyCorrect: The goal is a comparison with a twist: the stronger join is sometimes the wrong one. That needs the strength advantage of the splice, a drawback, and the situation in which the drawback decides. Choice A supplies all three — a splice keeps most of the strength, a knot costs about a third, but a splice cannot be cast off quickly, so a join that must be released is knotted.

whyWrong.B: This lists a cost of a knot and a cost of a splice, so it never establishes which join is stronger, and it draws no conclusion about what a rigger wants.
whyWrong.C: This is all in the splice's favour; without a drawback it cannot show why the weaker join is ever chosen.
whyWrong.D: This names two drawbacks of the splice but never says the splice is the stronger join, so the point that strength is being traded away is lost.

commonMistakes: Picking an option that is factually accurate but that answers a different goal than the one the stem states.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why the building is so long, so the answer must connect the length to a cause. Choice A does: rope was laid at full length, and the cables ran to about 200 metres, so the building had to be longer still. The other options report the length without explaining it.

whyWrong.B: This pairs the length with the fact that the building is still in use, which is interesting but is not a reason for the length.
whyWrong.C: This defines a ropewalk and gives a date; it never mentions why any particular ropewalk is long.
whyWrong.D: This gives the cable length and the building's present use but never links either to the ropewalk's dimensions.

tips: When the goal starts with "why," the correct option contains a causal word or clearly implies a cause.

whyCorrect: The reason clause is the key: a deformation can leave a diagram "looking utterly unlike" its original, so two pictures of the same knot may look completely different. Judging by eye will therefore often reach the wrong conclusion. "Unreliable" names that failure.

whyWrong.A: "Customary" would say eyeballing is the usual practice, which the sentence's because clause gives no support for.
whyWrong.B: Cost is irrelevant; the passage is about whether the judgement is correct, not what it takes to make it.
whyWrong.C: "Instantaneous" is about speed, and the problem the passage raises is accuracy.

tips: A blank introduced by "because" must be the consequence of the clause that follows it.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets a gain against a loss: paperbacks "gain speed of manufacture but _____ that behaviour." "That behaviour" is opening flat, which the sewn book has because it is not glued at the cut edge. Sawing off the folds and gluing destroys it, so the blank names giving something up.

whyWrong.A: "Predict" makes no sense of a binding method — a binding does not forecast how a book opens.
whyWrong.C: "Exaggerate" would mean paperbacks open even flatter, which reverses the contrast "but" sets up.
whyWrong.D: "Recover" would mean regaining the behaviour, but the glued edge is exactly what removes it.

tips: The conjunction "but" tells you the blank runs against the good thing named just before it.

whyCorrect: Confidence rose sharply; accuracy did not move at all. Two quantities that change without any tie between them are moving separately, and that is what "independently" means.

whyWrong.A: "Backwards" would require accuracy to fall, but the passage says the accounts simply did not improve.
whyWrong.B: "Reluctantly" describes an attitude, which cannot be a property of two measured quantities.
whyWrong.D: "Simultaneously" would mean they moved together, which is precisely what the second sentence denies.

commonMistakes: Reading "did not become more accurate" as "became less accurate"; no decline is reported.

whyCorrect: The passage says resistance carries an energy cost, so without the drug the resistant bacteria lose ground to their neighbours. Resistance only persists while the drug is there to make the cost worth paying. The blank contrasts with "acquired and kept," so it must mean actively maintained by the drug's presence.

whyWrong.A: "Disguised" would mean the resistance is hidden, but the passage is about whether it survives in the population, not whether it is detectable.
whyWrong.B: "Forbidden" by the drug reverses the biology — the drug is what favours resistant bacteria.
whyWrong.D: "Invented" suggests the drug creates the gene, but the passage describes selection among bacteria that already carry it.

tips: When a blank is set against a phrase like "not simply X but," it has to differ from X in a specific way the passage has already explained.

whyCorrect: The consequence given in the same sentence tells you the sense: the leaves have to be held down by hand. The over-tight spine is physically pushing the pages back up, opposing what the reader is trying to do. "Works against" captures that opposition.

whyWrong.A: "Declines to accept" is a refusal made by a person, and it needs something being offered — a spine refuses nothing.
whyWrong.B: "Survives damage from" is the endurance sense of the word, but the reader is not damaging the book.
whyWrong.D: "Endures" also means to withstand, and it would say the spine puts up with the reader rather than fighting back, which does not explain why the pages spring shut.

commonMistakes: Choosing the sense of "resist" you meet most often instead of the one the rest of the sentence requires.

whyCorrect: The text is built as a limit: here is what the method learns, here is a task it handles (a weather report), here is a task it cannot (a contract, where a term's meaning is fixed by a definition elsewhere). The final clause names why the line falls where it does — the system has no notion of reference. Marking that boundary is the purpose.

whyWrong.A: Collection and alignment of the corpora is never described; the passage takes the training data as given.
whyWrong.B: The text says nothing about who should do the translating, only about what this kind of system can do.
whyWrong.C: Only one kind of system is discussed, so there is no second system to compare it with.

commonMistakes: Turning a passage that describes a limitation into a recommendation the passage never makes.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence is the whole point: confidence tracks accuracy well at a first, untainted identification and poorly afterwards. The last sentence explains what breaks the link — feedback between the two moments. The text is sorting out when the relationship holds and when it does not.

whyWrong.A: Lineup procedure is not described; feedback is mentioned as what happens after an identification, not as a protocol.
whyWrong.B: No claim is made about how often identifications are wrong, only about when confidence is informative.
whyWrong.D: The passage identifies a condition rather than issuing an instruction to juries; it notes only that juries currently treat confidence as a measure.

tips: When a passage draws a line between two situations, its purpose is usually to locate that line, not to argue for a policy.

whyCorrect: The passage states the mechanism directly: a crust forms in minutes and insulates what is beneath it, so the interior stays fluid for weeks and keeps advancing. Fluid lava can keep moving; cooled lava stops. That insulation is the reason for the extra distance.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the opposite happens in the open — flows that spread stop sooner. A tube confines rather than spreads.
whyWrong.C: Slope is never mentioned; a tube does not change the gradient the lava runs down.
whyWrong.D: Gas escape is not discussed anywhere in the text.

tips: For an "according to the text" causal question, find the word so or because in the passage and read what follows it.

whyCorrect: The passage gives one valid inference and blocks its converse: different values prove different knots, but agreement on every quantity does not prove sameness. So the tool settles the "different" question and leaves the "same" question open.

whyWrong.A: The passage explicitly says that for a long while no known quantity could separate certain pairs, so computing more does not guarantee an answer.
whyWrong.B: One question is settled by the values alone — different values are decisive without any hand examination.
whyWrong.D: This is the reversal the passage rules out with the sentence "The reverse does not follow."

commonMistakes: Flipping the direction of a one-way implication; "different values means different knots" does not give you "same values means same knot."

whyCorrect: Chaudhuri's claim is about balancing two demands, so the evidence must address both columns. The table shows the settings tie on safety — 12 of 12 for each — and separate sharply on nuisance stops: 3 for the coarse setting against 47 for the fine. Equal safety with far fewer false trips is exactly a better balance.

whyWrong.A: This reports only the safety column, where the two settings are identical, so it gives no reason to prefer either.
whyWrong.C: This takes one number from each setting but from different columns, so the two figures are not comparable and no contrast is established.
whyWrong.D: This restates the definitions of the settings from the first column; definitions are not results.

tips: When an argument says one option "balances" two things, the supporting evidence has to touch both measures.

whyCorrect: Farrow says the difference does not show in a straight pull but does show under repeated loading. A supporting finding must therefore report near-equality in the straight pull and a clear gap under cycling. Choice D reports both halves.

whyWrong.A: Cost is not a mechanical property and says nothing about how either rope holds a load.
whyWrong.B: Water absorption is a different property altogether; Farrow's claim is about behaviour under repeated load.
whyWrong.C: That the ropes were made on the same machinery at the same twist is a control on the experiment, not a result.

commonMistakes: Accepting a finding that shows a difference of any kind, when the argument specifies which kind of test should and should not show one.

whyCorrect: Nwora's claim has two parts joined by "not only … but also": feedback changes confidence and changes what the witness reports about the original viewing. Choice D covers the second, harder part — witnesses recalled a longer, clearer view — and the phrase "although both groups had viewed it for the same time" rules out the possibility that the reports were simply accurate.

whyWrong.A: This supports only the confidence half of the claim, which is the part Nwora treats as already granted.
whyWrong.B: A general tendency to overestimate viewing time says nothing about the effect of feedback, since no comparison group is involved.
whyWrong.C: Who conducts the lineup is a separate variable; the number of identifications made does not bear on what witnesses later report.

tips: With a "not only … but also" claim, the correct evidence targets the "but also" clause.

whyCorrect: The first sentence supplies the consequence you need: a rope that has taken a set runs badly through a block. A rope coiled against its lay develops permanent kinks, which is a set that cannot be pulled out, so it must run through a block worse than a properly coiled rope.

whyWrong.B: Breaking strength is never discussed, and kinks give no reason to expect a rope to be stronger.
whyWrong.C: The passage compares coiling with the lay against coiling against it, not coiled against uncoiled storage — and kinking is taking a set faster, not more slowly.
whyWrong.D: Permanent kinks are defined in the passage as ones no amount of pulling will remove, so regaining the original shape contradicts the text.

tips: The blank continues a chain: find the sentence that states what the named condition causes, and apply it.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts two routes: a plasmid gene can cross between cells and between species without reproduction, while a chromosomal gene spreads only through descent. The same gene turning up in several unrelated species rules out descent as the route, so the plasmid route is what is left.

whyWrong.A: Differences in how much advantage the gene gives would explain how common it is, not how it reached unrelated species.
whyWrong.C: Independent origin in every species at once is exactly the coincidence the plasmid mechanism removes the need for, and the passage offers no support for it.
whyWrong.D: Long residence on each chromosome contradicts "unrelated species," since a chromosomal gene spreads only down a line of descent.

tips: When a passage sets out two mechanisms and then gives an observation, check which mechanism the observation excludes.

whyCorrect: "Braille's six-dot cell has sixty-three usable patterns" and "the alphabet, the digits, punctuation and a stock of contractions all fit inside that number" are both complete sentences with no conjunction between them. A semicolon is the mark that joins two independent clauses on its own.

whyWrong.A: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the two sentences fuse into one run-on.
whyWrong.C: A colon can introduce the second clause, but adding "and" after it stacks a second connector on top of the first.

commonMistakes: Seeing the list of items in the second half and assuming a colon-plus-list; the second half is a full sentence, not a list following an introduction.

whyCorrect: "A clergyman who worked for decades on tabulating knots" is a nonessential appositive describing Alexander Renshaw, and the sentence already supplies its closing comma after "knots." A nonessential element takes a matching comma at both ends, so the blank needs the opening comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "a clergyman who worked for decades on tabulating knots" is only a noun phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon paired with a comma gives the appositive two different marks, and the closing comma already in the sentence has to be matched by a comma, not a colon.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the appositive runs into the name, leaving "Alexander Renshaw a clergyman" without the break the closing comma implies.

tips: If you can see one comma already in place around an inserted description, the blank almost always needs its partner.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists three things the binder does: sews each gathering round three cords, laces the cord ends into the boards, and covers the whole in leather. Items in a series are separated by commas, so the blank takes the comma before "and" that closes the second item.

whyWrong.A: Leaving the comma out breaks the parallel punctuation of the series — the first item is already followed by one.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon separates items in a series only when the items themselves contain commas, and these do not.
whyWrong.D: A colon introduces a list, but the list here is already running and the colon would land in the middle of it.

tips: Count the verbs after the subject; three parallel verbs means a three-item series.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence, and "later ratings are worth much less" is another complete sentence. With no coordinating conjunction between them, a semicolon is the correct join.

whyWrong.A: A colon can precede an explanation, but "and" after it adds a second connector, and the resulting clause is joined twice.
whyWrong.C: A comma cannot join two independent clauses by itself; that is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With nothing between them the two sentences fuse.

commonMistakes: Being distracted by the comma earlier in the sentence, which belongs to the introductory phrase "before anyone has spoken to them" and does nothing for the join.

whyCorrect: The clause needs a finite verb, and with a "neither … nor" subject the verb agrees with the part nearer to it. The nearer part is the plural "the seam curves," so the plural tell us is required.

whyWrong.A: "Tells us" is singular, which would agree with "cloth grade" — the farther of the two subjects, not the nearer.
whyWrong.B: "Telling us" is a participle and leaves the sentence with no main verb.
whyWrong.C: An infinitive cannot be the main verb of the clause either.

tips: For neither/nor and either/or subjects, the verb matches whichever noun sits closest to it.

whyCorrect: The subject is "the yarns," which is plural; "that go into a strand of rope" is a relative clause describing it and does not change the subject. A plural subject in the present takes are.

whyWrong.A: "Was" is singular and past, so it fails on both number and the sentence's present-tense description of how rope is made.
whyWrong.B: "Has been" is singular, agreeing with "strand" or "rope" rather than with "yarns."
whyWrong.D: "Is" is singular and cannot take the plural subject "yarns."

commonMistakes: Letting the singular noun closest to the blank — "rope" — set the verb, when it belongs to the modifying clause rather than being the subject.

whyCorrect: The subject is the singular "a tarpaulin"; the words "that is lashed down over several open crates" form a relative clause, and "crates" is inside it, not the subject. A singular subject in the present tense takes shields.

whyWrong.A: "Shielding" is a participle, so the sentence would be left with no main verb.
whyWrong.B: "Have shielded" is plural and shifts the sentence into the present perfect, while the comparison with a loose sheet is a general present-tense statement.
whyWrong.D: "Shield" is the plural form and would agree with "crates," which is not the subject.

tips: Strip out any clause beginning with that, which, or who before deciding the verb's number.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the old convention — size stated as the distance round the rope. The second gives a different convention, the distance across, and shows the same rope getting a very different number. The two systems are set against each other, so the transition must mark opposition.

whyWrong.B: "For instance" would make the modern lists an example of the old girth measurement, but they use the opposite measurement.
whyWrong.C: "In addition" would add a second point in the same direction; here the second sentence replaces the first convention rather than extending it.
whyWrong.D: "As a result" would make the modern practice a consequence of the old one, and nothing in the passage says the change followed from measuring girth.

tips: When the same object gets two different numbers in two sentences, the link is contrast.

whyCorrect: "A netmaker at work measures nothing" leads you to expect uneven meshes. The next sentence says every mesh comes out the same size anyway, and only then explains the gauge that makes it possible. The transition has to concede the first fact and then defy the expectation it raises.

whyWrong.A: "For that reason" would make uniform mesh a consequence of not measuring, which is backwards.
whyWrong.B: "In much the same way" claims a parallel, but the two sentences point in opposite directions.
whyWrong.C: "To begin with" signals the first item in a sequence, and nothing else in the passage continues a list.

commonMistakes: Reading the "because" clause as the connection between the sentences; it explains how the surprising result happens, which is why the surprise still needs marking.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says agreement between invariants leaves the question open; the second says disagreement settles it at once. Inconclusive against decisive is a direct opposition, so a contrast transition is needed.

whyWrong.A: "Consequently" would make the decisive case follow from the inconclusive one, but neither causes the other.
whyWrong.B: "In short" introduces a summary, and the second sentence adds a new and opposite fact rather than condensing the first.
whyWrong.D: "Likewise" claims the two cases behave alike, which is exactly what the passage denies.

tips: Look for a pair of opposed words across the two sentences — here "leaves open" against "settles at once."

whyCorrect: To show that neither kind is better in itself you need a benefit, a matching cost, and the uses that follow from each. Choice B gives tar's advantage (keeps damp out), its price (stiffer and weaker), and then both applications, so the choice is shown to depend on the job rather than on quality.

whyWrong.A: This names the two uses but omits the trade-off that explains them, so it reads as two arbitrary customs rather than an argument.
whyWrong.C: This is only the fact that both types exist; nothing is compared.
whyWrong.D: This lists only tar's advantages, which suggests tarred cordage is simply better — the opposite of the goal.

tips: A goal phrased as "neither is better in itself" needs an advantage and a disadvantage in the same sentence.

whyCorrect: The goal is to describe the process. Choice C actually walks through it: spun in place, a wheel carrying wires back and forth, then compacting and wrapping once all the wires are laid. The other options report facts about cables without saying how one is built.

whyWrong.A: Duration and a single later step are given, but the spinning itself — the wheel crossing the span — is missing.
whyWrong.B: This says only where the work happens, not what the work consists of.
whyWrong.D: A wire count and a duration are statistics about cables, not a description of the process.

tips: For a "describe the process" goal, count the steps the option contains; the winner usually has the most of them in order.

whyCorrect: The goal names both partners, so the sentence must state what each side gets. Choice A gives the fungus sugar from the tree's leaves and gives the tree phosphorus from pores no root can reach, which also explains why the tree cannot get it alone.

whyWrong.B: This states where the fungus lives and reports an experiment; neither says what either partner receives.
whyWrong.C: This covers only the fungus's access to the pores and never mentions what the tree gives in return.
whyWrong.D: The seedling experiment shows the partnership matters but says nothing about what is exchanged.

commonMistakes: Choosing the note that sounds most like evidence when the goal asks for an explanation of an exchange.

whyCorrect: The passage describes wires being laid one at a time by a travelling wheel until the bundle is thick enough, then squeezed and bound. That is building the cable out of parts at the site, and the sentence contrasts it with being "delivered." "Assembled" is the word for putting something together from parts.

whyWrong.A: "Concealed" would mean hidden, and nothing in the passage hides the cable.
whyWrong.B: "Replaced" implies an earlier cable was there first, which the passage never suggests.
whyWrong.D: "Inspected" describes checking finished work, not the construction the passage details.

tips: The contrast at the end of the sentence — "rather than delivered" — tells you the blank names how the cable came to exist.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says a single fibre's breaking load "varies a good deal from fibre to fibre." The second says the rope is "steadier" because load transfers to neighbours. The blank must name the opposite of that variability, and predictability is what low variation gives you.

whyWrong.B: "Impressive" is a judgement about how strong the rope seems, while the passage is about how consistent the strength is.
whyWrong.C: Cost is never raised in the passage.
whyWrong.D: "Familiar" concerns how well known something is, not how much it varies.

commonMistakes: Reading the passage as a claim that the rope is stronger; the stated contrast is steadiness, not magnitude.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts two kinds of work. In the old approach the labour was writing out rules — "stating the language." In the new one the system finds regularities itself, so the human work left is assembling the millions of already-translated sentences it learns from. "Gathering" names that work.

whyWrong.A: Nothing suggests the examples are shortened; their number is what makes them useful.
whyWrong.B: "Disputing" the examples would be arguing about them, which no part of the passage describes.
whyWrong.C: The examples were "already translated by people," so translating them is not the new labour — it is what made them available in the first place.

commonMistakes: Choosing "translating" because the topic is translation; the sentence asks what humans do to the examples, and the passage says they already exist.

whyCorrect: The passage explains that the yarns had to be stretched to full length, so the building had to match the rope's length. The blank is set against "not a matter of style," so it must name something the process forced. "Consequence" states that the shape follows from the work done inside.

whyWrong.B: A building's shape cannot be a criticism of the process it houses, and no fault-finding appears in the text.
whyWrong.C: "Rejection" would mean the shape refused the process, but the shape was dictated by it.
whyWrong.D: "Decoration" is a form of style, which the sentence has just ruled out.

tips: When a blank follows "not X but," it must be a genuine opposite of X, not another version of it.

whyCorrect: The passage states the direction of transfer confidently — sugar moves from the plant that has more to the plant that has less — and then raises a question it does not answer: whether the mature tree gets anything back. "Remains _____" needs a word for an open question, and "unsettled" is it.

whyWrong.A: "Unpublished" would be a claim about the literature, and the passage says nothing about what has been printed.
whyWrong.B: "Unpopular" describes how people feel about an idea, not whether a fact is known.
whyWrong.C: "Unavoidable" would say the tree definitely gains, which turns the open question into an answer.

tips: "Remains" plus a blank usually signals an unresolved question, so scan for the option that means "still not known."

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence states a general rule — every twist opposes the twist below it. The sentences that follow trace that rule through the actual layers: fibres to yarn one way, yarns to strands the other, strands back again into rope, and then the consequence that the rope holds itself together. That is a principle followed by its working-out.

whyWrong.A: No objection is raised; nothing in the text disagrees with the underlined sentence or rebuts it.
whyWrong.B: The relationship runs the other way — the underlined sentence is the general statement and what follows is the detail.
whyWrong.C: A conclusion needs evidence before it, and the underlined sentence is the first sentence of the passage proper.

tips: Check what sits before the underlined sentence; a sentence with nothing before it cannot be concluding from earlier evidence.

whyCorrect: The first sentence asserts a shortfall: rope strength is not fibre strength times fibre count. The underlined sentence supplies the reason in compressed form — the fibres do not fail simultaneously — and the following sentences unpack it into the cascade. It is the hinge from the claim to its explanation.

whyWrong.A: It is not a restatement; the opening sentence says nothing about the timing of breaks, which is the new information the underlined sentence adds.
whyWrong.C: It supports rather than qualifies what comes later; the cascade description depends on it.
whyWrong.D: Far from being a counterexample, it is the premise the cascade in the final sentence is built on.

commonMistakes: Labelling any short sentence a restatement; compare the actual content of the two sentences before deciding.

whyCorrect: The passage links speed to reading whole words as patterns, gives that as the reason contracted braille is taught from the start, and then concedes the uncontracted form is easier to learn but slower, with a habit that must later be unlearned. Taken together that is a cost weighed against a benefit, with the benefit winning.

whyWrong.B: The passage says the contracted form is taught first in most schools, not that the uncontracted form has disappeared.
whyWrong.C: No comparison with sighted readers appears anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.D: The order in which the two forms were developed is never discussed; the passage is about teaching order, not invention.

tips: A main-idea answer should account for both halves of a passage that concedes something — here the ease of learning as well as the speed.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets out the trade in both directions: the fungus takes sugar and passes back phosphorus from soil the roots could never reach. The question asks what the tree gains, so the answer is the phosphorus.

whyWrong.A: Protection from drying out is not mentioned; the benefit named is a nutrient, not moisture.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the exchange — the sugar goes from the tree to the fungus, and the tree's own leaves make it.
whyWrong.C: The seedling experiment held light constant between the groups, and the passage never claims growth without light.

commonMistakes: Reversing the direction of an exchange; underline who gives and who receives before answering.

whyCorrect: Elstad claims the survivors are not genetically different, only dormant. If survival came from a resistance gene, the regrown population would be measurably harder to kill the second time and would pass that on. Choice C reports exactly the opposite — no extra resistance in the survivors, and descendants dying at the usual rate — which is what a purely temporary, non-genetic escape predicts.

whyWrong.A: Finding resistance genes before treatment supports the conventional explanation Elstad is arguing against.
whyWrong.B: That larger doses kill more cells is true under either explanation and does not distinguish them.
whyWrong.D: A slower recovery says something about growth rate, not about whether the survivors carry a resistance gene.

tips: To test a "not genetic" claim, look for evidence about the survivors' offspring, since a genetic trait would be inherited.

whyCorrect: Naess's claim is about where the carbon ends up: mostly in the fungus, not in a second tree. Labelling carbon and then tracking it settles that directly — large amounts recovered in fungal tissue and only traces in the connected seedlings is the distribution her argument predicts.

whyWrong.A: How much carbon leaves the tree says nothing about its destination, which is the whole point at issue.
whyWrong.C: Faster growth in connected seedlings suggests they do benefit, which cuts against Naess rather than supporting her.
whyWrong.D: The number of species a network links describes its extent, not how the carbon inside it is divided up.

tips: When a claim is about a destination, the useful evidence measures the same quantity at two possible endpoints.

whyCorrect: Liest says the hearth dates are too early to date the paintings. The only way to show that is to date the paintings themselves and compare. Choice A does exactly that: pigment from the figures gives dates thousands of years later than the charcoal below, so the fires came first and cannot date the art.

whyWrong.B: Burnt bone in the hearths tells you what was burned, not when the wall was painted.
whyWrong.C: Hearths in undecorated chambers show that fires and paintings are not always found together, but it puts no date on this chamber's figures.
whyWrong.D: Precision in the charcoal date strengthens the hearth date; the argument is that the date belongs to the wrong event, not that it is imprecise.

commonMistakes: Confusing a date that is inaccurate with a date that is accurate but measures the wrong thing.

whyCorrect: The passage grants the invariant full theoretical power — it separates every pair yet tabulated — and then says the computation grows so steeply that even modest diagrams are out of reach. Restrict that to knots with many crossings and the invariant works in principle but cannot be used. That is the gap between power and practicality.

whyWrong.A: The passage says it distinguishes every pair tabulated, so its discriminating power is not the failing.
whyWrong.C: Being unusable at large sizes is the opposite of being the one to rely on.
whyWrong.D: Nothing equates the invariant with a crossing count; crossing number is only what makes it expensive to compute.

tips: When a passage concedes a strength and then names an obstacle, the completion usually holds both together.

whyCorrect: The passage gives you a signal — ground above a shallow tube is warmer than ground beside it — and says the difference lasts while lava is still moving. A thermal survey from the air detects exactly that signal, so it can follow the warm line and map the tube without touching it.

whyWrong.B: A temperature difference is not a flow measurement; the passage gives no way to convert warmth into a volume of lava.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text says where new tubes form, only how existing ones show at the surface.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the warmth persists only while lava is moving, which means drained tubes can be told apart from the air — excavation is precisely what is not needed.

commonMistakes: Stretching the inference beyond the one property the passage measured; detecting heat is not the same as quantifying flow.

whyCorrect: "Each one already galvanised and tested before it leaves the mill" is a modifier attached to "coils" by the comma that is already in the sentence, and inside that modifier "each one" is the noun being described. No further punctuation belongs between the noun and its description.

whyWrong.B: A second comma cuts "each one" off from the words that describe it, leaving a noun phrase dangling with no completion.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon joins independent clauses, and "already galvanised and tested before it leaves the mill" has no subject-verb pair of its own.
whyWrong.D: A period demands a full sentence after it, and "Already galvanised and tested before it leaves the mill" is a fragment.

tips: Before adding a mark, check whether the part after it could stand alone; if it cannot, most heavy punctuation is wrong.

whyCorrect: The first part, "A parallel corpus is not simply two texts in two languages," is a complete sentence, and what follows spells out what more is required. A colon after a complete clause introduces that kind of explanation.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon already links two independent clauses, so adding "and" gives the sentence two joins where one is needed.
whyWrong.C: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse into a run-on.

tips: A colon is the right choice when the second half answers the question "which is to say what?" raised by the first.

whyCorrect: "Because the mesh of a safety net must stretch as the load comes on" begins with because, so it is a dependent clause opening the sentence. An introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma before the main clause begins.

whyWrong.A: A colon has to follow a complete sentence, and a because-clause is not one.
whyWrong.C: Without any mark the dependent clause runs into "it is," so the reader loses the boundary.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and the first half here cannot stand alone.

commonMistakes: Assuming a long opening stretch is independent; the subordinating word at the front settles it.

whyCorrect: "The sailmaker draws the seam curves full size on the loft floor, then lays the cloth over the drawing and marks them" is a complete sentence, and "the panels are cut only when every line has been checked" is another. With no coordinating conjunction between them, a semicolon makes the join.

whyWrong.A: A comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: With no mark at all the two sentences run together.
whyWrong.C: A colon followed by "and" pairs two connectors, and the second clause is a new statement rather than an explanation of "marks them."

tips: Read from the blank to the end: if that stretch is a full sentence, a comma alone can never be the answer.

whyCorrect: The sentence names exactly two diagrams, and the subject of the clause is the singular "each." When one of a pair is the subject, the remaining member is "the other" — singular and definite.

whyWrong.A: "The others" is plural and would require three or more diagrams; only two are in play.
whyWrong.C: "Another" means one more of an unspecified group, which suggests a third diagram that does not exist here.
whyWrong.D: "Each other" is a reciprocal pronoun that needs a plural subject, but the subject is the singular "each," so the two forms clash.

tips: Count the items first: two takes "the other," three or more takes "the others" or "another."

whyCorrect: The opening participial phrase "Having laid the wires one at a time across the span" is not a clause, so the main clause after the comma still needs its own finite verb. "The compacting machine" is a singular subject in the present tense, which takes squeezes.

whyWrong.B: "Squeezing" is another participle, so the sentence would consist of two modifiers and no main verb.
whyWrong.C: An infinitive cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence.
whyWrong.D: "Having squeezed" is a perfect participle, which again leaves the subject with nothing to do.

tips: An opening phrase that begins with an -ing or having form is never the sentence's main verb; the blank after the comma usually is.

whyCorrect: The comparison is between two groups of bacteria, and the second half needs a noun phrase to serve as the subject of "do." The possessive must be plural to agree with "bacteria," giving "their neighbours."

whyWrong.A: "Its" is singular and cannot refer back to the plural "bacteria."
whyWrong.C: "Them" is an object pronoun, but the blank is the subject of the verb "do."
whyWrong.D: "Theirs" is a possessive pronoun standing alone, so "than theirs do" leaves the comparison without a noun to name the other group.

commonMistakes: Comparing a group to a possession instead of to another group; check what the verb after the blank needs as its subject.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a fact about the material — new canvas shrinks when wetted, by nearly an inch a yard. The second gives what follows from it for a tarpaulin cut to exact size. Cause then consequence calls for a resultative transition.

whyWrong.A: "Similarly" would introduce a second parallel case, but the second sentence is the outcome of the first, not a companion to it.
whyWrong.B: "Meanwhile" marks two things happening at the same time and ignores the causal link.
whyWrong.D: "Nonetheless" signals that the second sentence resists the first, whereas it follows straight from it.

tips: If you can insert "so" between the two sentences and the meaning holds, you need a result transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence names a problem: standing rigging chafes where it crosses a spar or another rope. The second gives the practice adopted because of it — winding the exposed length with tarred twine so the twine wears through first. That is a response to the stated cause.

whyWrong.A: "Even so" would concede the chafing and then describe something happening despite it, but wrapping the rope is a direct answer to the chafing.
whyWrong.B: "In contrast" requires opposition, and the second sentence supports rather than opposes the first.
whyWrong.C: "Beforehand" reverses the order — the wrapping is a response to the problem, not something prior to it.

tips: A sentence describing what people do about a problem just stated is nearly always signalled by a result transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the mechanics — opposite twists, each layer holding the one inside it. The second restates what that amounts to: nothing holds the rope together except its own internal tension. A transition that marks a summing-up of what the mechanism means is what fits.

whyWrong.A: "By contrast" needs an opposition, and the second sentence agrees with the first.
whyWrong.B: "For instance" would make the second sentence a specific case, but it is a general conclusion about the whole rope.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" would mean the second sentence holds despite the first, when it is a direct consequence of it.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a contrast word because the second sentence starts with "nothing"; the negative wording still states agreement.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why the brake acts when nothing else does, so the answer needs the mechanism and the absence of any external trigger. Choice C gives both: weights on the cage press outward as it descends, bite into the rails past a set speed, and no driver signal or circuit is involved.

whyWrong.A: Naming where the weights are mounted does not explain how they act or why no signal is needed.
whyWrong.B: This gives half the mechanism and then swaps in a historical fact, dropping the point about no circuit being involved.
whyWrong.D: A date and an inventor say nothing about how the brake works.

tips: When a goal contains "why … even when," the answer must include the fact that makes the "even when" true.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why timing does not work. Choice B supplies the reason — the rate depends on water temperature, so no fixed number of days suits every batch — and adds the penalty at both ends, fibre that will not part and fibre that crumbles. That is a cause plus its consequences.

whyWrong.A: This restates the practice without giving any reason for it, which is exactly what the goal asks for.
whyWrong.C: This defines retting and never touches on timing.
whyWrong.D: This gives only the over-soaking failure, leaving out the variable rate that makes a fixed schedule impossible.

tips: A "why" goal is not satisfied by a note that describes what is done; look for the note that explains the variability.

whyCorrect: The decline needs a mechanism, and the notes supply one: the protein costs energy that would have gone into growth, so once the drug is gone the resistant strains are outgrown. Choice D links the cost to the outcome in a single causal sentence.

whyWrong.A: This pairs a fact about drug presence with the bare observation that resistance declines, and never says why it declines.
whyWrong.B: This gives the energy cost but stops before connecting it to what happens in the population after withdrawal.
whyWrong.C: This is the phenomenon itself restated, with no explanation attached.

commonMistakes: Picking the note that matches the goal's wording most closely; the goal asks for the cause, not the effect it names.

whyCorrect: The key detail is the depth: the paint is grey-black at the surface but still red a fraction of a millimetre down, and the change happens only where light reaches. The blank is set against "the pigment ageing throughout," so it must mean confined to the surface. "Superficial" is that word in its literal sense.

whyWrong.A: "Gradual" describes rate, not depth, and the sentence contrasts a surface effect with a change running through the whole layer.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the passage says the grey-black can be turned back to red.
whyWrong.C: The darkening ruins the appearance of the paint, and in any case harm is not the contrast the sentence sets up.

commonMistakes: Taking "superficial" only in its figurative sense of trivial; here it means literally at the surface.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts two processes by what each gives up. Grinding keeps nearly all the wood, so more paper per tonne — the cheap option. Chemical cooking halves the yield but produces fibres that are longer and far less brittle, and long unbrittle fibres are what make a strong sheet. The blank names the benefit bought at the cost of yield.

whyWrong.A: Thickness is never mentioned; both processes can make sheets of any weight.
whyWrong.B: Whiteness is a matter of bleaching, which the passage does not raise.
whyWrong.D: Smoothness comes from finishing the surface, and the passage's contrast is about fibre length and brittleness.

tips: Pick the blank from the property the passage actually measured — here fibre length and brittleness, which is strength.

whyCorrect: The passage explicitly says the residue was not what set Perkin apart — a hundred like it were washed away. What he did instead was test it: he dyed silk, sent it out for an expert opinion, and patented it. The blank names that follow-up investigation.

whyWrong.A: The coincidence is the accident itself, which the sentence has just ruled out as the distinguishing factor.
whyWrong.C: Publicity would come after the patent; the actions described are private tests and a professional consultation.
whyWrong.D: Cost is never mentioned, and spending money is not what the listed actions have in common.

tips: When a sentence says "not X but the _____ that followed it," the blank must name the actions described just before.

whyCorrect: The passage lists what beating decides: bulky and opaque but weak, or hard, translucent and strong. Those are qualities of the finished sheet, not measurements of it. The closing contrast — "rather than a preparation for making it" — means the beater settles what kind of paper it is, which is its character.

whyWrong.B: Cost is never discussed; the variables named are roll weight and running time as controls on quality, not price.
whyWrong.C: Size is fixed by the mould and the machine, and none of the properties listed is a dimension.
whyWrong.D: Colour appears nowhere in the passage; opacity and translucency are not colour.

commonMistakes: Reading "opaque" and "translucent" as colour terms; they describe how light passes through the sheet.

whyCorrect: The passage says pages painted with verdigris are pierced clean through and that the copper salt attacks the cellulose beneath it. The blank describes the pigment's relation to the page, and active destruction is what "hostile" names.

whyWrong.B: "Indifferent" would mean the pigment leaves the page alone, which the holes in the parchment flatly contradict.
whyWrong.C: "Superior" compares quality between two things; the sentence is about what the pigment does to the page.
whyWrong.D: "Essential" would make the pigment necessary to the page, the reverse of destroying it.

tips: The word "but" hidden in the structure — prized for brilliance, yet destructive — tells you the blank is negative.

whyCorrect: The sentence before names logwood's defects — the colour needs an iron salt to strike and greys within a few years. The underlined sentence reports the statutory ban, and the sentence after says the ban lasted until dyers could fix the colour. So the underlined sentence is the official reaction to the fault just described.

whyWrong.A: Where logwood was cut and how it was shipped is never mentioned; the sentence is about a prohibition on importing it.
whyWrong.C: The remedy is named in the following sentence — fixing the colour with chrome — not in the underlined one.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the sentence casts doubt on the defect; the ban treats it as real.

tips: For a function question, read one sentence either side and describe the underlined sentence's relation to both.

whyCorrect: The text spends its length on how amate departs from the familiar method — no pulp, nothing suspended in water, nothing drained, no mould, no fixed size — and then insists in the last sentence that it is still paper, judged by what it does. That is one product reached by an unfamiliar route.

whyWrong.B: The final sentence says the opposite: amate is paper by what it does.
whyWrong.C: No geography or spread is traced; the passage describes a technique, not its distribution.
whyWrong.D: Durability is never compared, and European paper is not mentioned.

commonMistakes: Letting the long list of things amate does not do lead you to a conclusion the passage explicitly rejects.

whyCorrect: The passage moves in three steps: paint had to be ground daily and spoiled overnight, the 1841 tube kept it usable for months and portable, and painters consequently carried whole pictures outdoors instead of working from sketches. The storage change is the cause and the change of location is the effect.

whyWrong.A: The passage gives no evidence about the inventor's intent; it reports what followed, not what was aimed at.
whyWrong.C: Quality is never compared — the contrast is between paint that hardened overnight and paint that kept.
whyWrong.D: The text says painters had worked out of doors from sketches, so outdoor work was already established.

tips: When a passage names a before, an invention, and an after, the main idea is the causal link between them.

whyCorrect: The passage says anthocyanins shift colour with the acidity of the surrounding sap and with the metal ions bound to them, so one pigment covers red, purple and blue. The hydrangea example makes the point explicit: liming does not supply a new pigment, it changes how the existing one behaves. The environment, not the molecule, does the work.

whyWrong.B: No second pigment is mentioned; the passage insists the same class of molecule is responsible in each case.
whyWrong.C: Petal thickness is never raised anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.D: Age at picking plays no part in the explanation the passage gives.

tips: When a passage offers a worked example, check your answer against it — the hydrangea sentence rules out any "different pigment" option.

whyCorrect: Two conditions have to be met at once: drying within four hours and spread of no more than 0.4 mm. Check each row. Ink 1 dries in 2.5 hours but spreads 0.7. Ink 3 spreads only 0.2 but takes 6.0 hours. Ink 4 spreads 0.6. Only ink 2, at 3.5 hours and 0.3 mm, clears both limits.

whyWrong.A: Ink 4 dries in time but spreads 0.6 mm, which exceeds the 0.4 mm limit.
whyWrong.C: Ink 3 has the least spread but takes 6.0 hours, well over the four-hour limit.
whyWrong.D: Ink 1 is the fastest to dry but spreads 0.7 mm, the worst of the four on that measure.

commonMistakes: Choosing the row that wins on one column; a two-condition requirement disqualifies any ink that fails either one.

whyCorrect: The sentence compares two specific steps, 60 to 80 and 80 to 98, so the data must cover exactly those. Uptake goes 71 to 92, a gain of 21 points, then 92 to 95, a gain of 3. Those two numbers are what make the comparison true.

whyWrong.A: The highest value at 98 degrees says nothing about how much was gained getting there.
whyWrong.B: The 40-to-60 step is a different pair of temperatures from the two the sentence compares.
whyWrong.D: The value at 40 degrees is outside the range under discussion.

tips: When a claim names two intervals, take the difference across each one rather than reading single values.

whyCorrect: Bao says the report was written to blame the binding rather than the handling. The quotation must therefore point at a structural feature and away from human contact. Choice B does both at once: the tear always starts at the joint where the leather has failed, and not at the fore-edge a hand touches.

whyWrong.A: Shelving and its distance from the wall concern storage conditions, not binding or handling.
whyWrong.C: Windows and heating describe the room's environment, which is a third cause the claim does not involve.
whyWrong.D: The number of volumes and days records the scale of the survey, not the cause of any damage.

tips: A quotation supports a two-sided claim best when it affirms one side and denies the other in the same breath.

whyCorrect: The half-treated sheet is the decisive experiment. The bath and the floating colour are identical for both halves, and only the sheet differs, yet the colour survives the rinse on the treated half alone. So whatever the alum does, it does to the paper.

whyWrong.A: The sheet is rinsed and still handled wet, so it plainly takes up water; the passage never claims the alum waterproofs it.
whyWrong.C: The bath's thickness is a property of the bath, and the half-and-half result shows the difference lies in the sheet.
whyWrong.D: Brightness is never measured; the passage is about whether the colour stays put through a rinse.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the one-half-only sentence, which is the only detail that separates an effect on the paper from an effect on the bath.

whyCorrect: The passage stresses that the stick "carries no water at all," that water is added only at the moment of use, and that a bottled liquid version goes mouldy within a season while a two-hundred-year-old stick still works. Mould needs water, so keeping the ink dry is what removes the limit on storage.

whyWrong.A: Depth of black is never compared between stick ink and bottled ink.
whyWrong.B: Only one pigment, lampblack, is named, and nothing suggests the solid form widens the choice.
whyWrong.C: How the ink is applied is not discussed; the stick is rubbed on a stone to make ink, not used as a writing tool.

tips: The word "therefore" points back to the contrast just drawn — here two centuries against one season.

whyCorrect: "The colouring matter of the madder root" is a nonessential appositive naming alizarin, and the sentence already has its opening comma after "Alizarin." A nonessential element needs a comma at both ends, so the blank supplies the closing one.

whyWrong.A: A colon must follow a complete sentence, and "Alizarin, the colouring matter of the madder root" has no verb yet.
whyWrong.C: With no closing comma the appositive is left unbalanced, with one comma opening it and nothing closing it.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and what precedes it here is only a noun phrase.

tips: An interrupter takes matching marks — if you can see a comma opening it, the blank closing it is a comma too.

whyCorrect: "The rule the old colourmen are said to have taught their apprentices was short" is a complete sentence, and what follows states the rule itself. A colon after a complete clause is the mark for introducing the specific content that the clause has just announced.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "short grind" reads as a single phrase and the rule runs into the description of it.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon links two clauses of equal weight, but the second half here spells out the first rather than standing beside it.
whyWrong.D: A comma is too weak to introduce the imperative clause, which can stand on its own as a sentence.

tips: When the first clause promises something — a rule, a reason, a list — and the second delivers it, use a colon.

whyCorrect: "Grinding that powder turned it red" and "indeed, the change was so unlike anything else in the trade …" are both complete sentences, and indeed is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction. Two independent clauses joined by a conjunctive adverb take a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

whyWrong.A: Even if a colon could introduce the second clause, "indeed" as a sentence adverb still needs its following comma, which this option omits.
whyWrong.C: A comma before "indeed" leaves two independent clauses joined by nothing stronger than a comma — a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: "Red indeed" reads as intensifying the colour, and the two clauses are then fused with no boundary between them.

tips: However, therefore, indeed and moreover are adverbs, not conjunctions; they cannot join two sentences with a comma.

whyCorrect: "Which is the last engine of its kind at work anywhere in the country" is a nonessential relative clause commenting on the beater, and it begins with which. A nonessential clause is set off with a comma.

whyWrong.A: Without a comma the clause reads as essential, but a which clause supplying extra information needs the comma, and the sentence would run on unpunctuated.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and a clause beginning with "which" is subordinate.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation or a list, and a relative clause is neither.

tips: A relative clause opening with "which" and adding non-defining information takes a comma; a defining clause would use "that" and no comma.

whyCorrect: "Beaten for four hours instead of one" is a participial phrase, and the noun it modifies has to be the first thing after the comma. The thing that gets beaten is the pulp, not the papermaker, the sheet or an abstract quality, so only the option that opens with "the pulp" attaches the modifier correctly.

whyWrong.A: This says the papermaker was beaten for four hours.
whyWrong.B: This makes the sheet the thing beaten, but the beating happens to the pulp before there is a sheet — the sheet is the result.
whyWrong.C: This makes "hardness and translucency" the things beaten, which is not something that can be beaten at all.

commonMistakes: Judging these by which sentence sounds smoothest instead of asking which noun the opening phrase can logically describe.

whyCorrect: The subject of the sentence is each, and "of the four vats" is a prepositional phrase that cannot contain the subject. Each is always singular, so the verb is is. The sense agrees: the vats are started one at a time.

whyWrong.A: "Were" is plural and also shifts the sentence into the past, while the passage describes the mill's standing practice.
whyWrong.B: "Have been" is plural and present perfect, agreeing with "vats" rather than with "each."
whyWrong.D: "Are" is plural, drawn by the nearby "four vats" instead of the actual subject.

tips: Cross out any phrase beginning with "of" before choosing the verb — the subject is never inside it.

whyCorrect: There are three painters and the orders belong to them, so the noun must be both plural and possessive. A plural noun already ending in -s takes an apostrophe after the s: painters'.

whyWrong.A: "Painter's" is singular possessive, which contradicts "all three."
whyWrong.B: "Painters" is plural but not possessive, so the orders are not shown to belong to anyone.
whyWrong.C: "Painters's" doubles the s; a regular plural ending in -s takes only the apostrophe.

tips: Decide plural first, then add possession: painters, then painters'.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the ink is as black now as when it was written. The second says the paper has browned, so what a reader sees is not what the scribe saw. The second sentence undercuts the impression the first creates, which calls for a contrast transition.

whyWrong.B: "Therefore" would make the browning a consequence of the ink's permanence, and the two are independent.
whyWrong.C: "Furthermore" adds a point in the same direction, but the browning works against the ink's unchanged blackness.
whyWrong.D: "For instance" would make the paper an example of the ink not fading, which it is not.

tips: When the second sentence complicates a good-news first sentence, you need "however" or an equivalent.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the physical operations — sections sewn to cords, cord ends laced into boards. The second restates what those operations amount to: boards, sewing and sections form one structure. A transition marking a summary of what has just been described is what fits.

whyWrong.A: "For example" would make the second sentence one instance of the first, but it is a general conclusion about the whole binding.
