whyWrong.B: "Earlier" claims the second sentence describes a prior stage, and no time order is involved.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" signals opposition, and the second sentence agrees with the first.

commonMistakes: Confusing "in effect" with "in fact"; here it means the described operations add up to a single structure.

whyCorrect: The first sentence is a failure — mauve faded and went out of fashion within a decade. The second is a success on a much larger scale, several hundred coal-tar colours by 1900. The transition has to concede the failure and then set the success against it.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" claims the two sentences point the same way, but one records a collapse and the other an expansion.
whyWrong.B: "Meanwhile" marks simultaneity, and the two facts are separated by decades rather than happening at once.
whyWrong.D: "In short" introduces a summary, and the second sentence brings in new information that the first does not contain.

tips: When one sentence is a setback and the next is a success that came anyway, the link is concession.

whyCorrect: "In spite of its difficulty" means the sentence has to hold two things together: what made the process hard and what made it worth doing anyway. Choice A gives the dozen-plus steps and three months as the cost and the colour surviving decades of washing as the payoff.

whyWrong.B: This lists an origin and one unpleasant step, so it is all difficulty and no reason to accept it.
whyWrong.C: That chemists could not explain the oil steps is another obstacle rather than a benefit.
whyWrong.D: This is a bare definition of Turkey red and mentions neither the difficulty nor the reward.

tips: A goal containing "in spite of" needs an option with a concession and a benefit in the same sentence.

whyCorrect: The goal is the purpose of the tail, so the sentence has to say what the tail does. Choice A traces it through: knotted under the belt, book hanging at the side, and coming up the right way round when lifted to be read. That is the design working.

whyWrong.B: Survival numbers and paintings are evidence about how the books are known today, not what the tail was for.
whyWrong.C: This describes the tail's appearance and position but stops before saying what it accomplishes.
whyWrong.D: This says where the book was carried without connecting it to the tail or explaining the upside-down hanging.

commonMistakes: Settling for the note that mentions the object; a purpose question needs the note that says what it achieves.

whyCorrect: The report is taken seriously because independent physical evidence agrees with it. Choice C sets the report's weakness — a single uncorroborated account — against the analysis of surviving balls, which found the very compound that the described diet would produce. That corroboration is the reason.

whyWrong.A: The end of the trade and the absence of other accounts explain why the report stands alone, which is a reason for doubt, not confidence.
whyWrong.B: This restates the report's content without offering any support for it.
whyWrong.D: The pigment's appearance and origin say nothing about whether the account of its manufacture is true.

tips: "Why is X believed" is answered by evidence from outside X, not by repeating what X says.

whyCorrect: The passage explains that a continuous pattern across the closed edges is broken if a leaf is removed or added. Libraries valued that not for looks — the sentence says so directly — but because tampering became easy to see. "Plain" here means apparent to the eye.

whyWrong.A: "Unadorned" is the decorative sense, and the sentence explicitly sets aside appearance as the reason.
whyWrong.C: "Ordinary" would mean interference was common, which is not what the marbling accomplishes.
whyWrong.D: "Modest" describes restraint in style, again the appearance sense the sentence rules out.

commonMistakes: Choosing the visual sense of "plain" because the passage is about decoration; the clause "less for their appearance than" is the warning against it.

whyCorrect: The contrast in the passage is about removability: the starch mend comes off with water, the synthetic one needs solvents that damage the leaf. A mend that can be taken off leaves the next conservator free to choose. "Reversed" is the word for undoing a treatment cleanly.

whyWrong.A: "Untied" applies to knots and fastenings, and a pasted repair is not tied.
whyWrong.B: "Ruined" would make the mend's failure the point, but the passage praises the possibility of removing it deliberately.
whyWrong.C: "Neglected" means left unattended, which has nothing to do with whether a repair can be taken out.

tips: Substitute each option into the sentence and check it still explains the reason given — only "reversed" gives the next generation a choice.

whyCorrect: The blank is paired with "its worst weakness," so it must name the advantage of the same property. The advantage the passage gives is practical: the painter can lift a passage out of a wash weeks later. That is a convenience the medium offers the painter.

whyWrong.A: Expense is a cost, not an advantage, and price is never mentioned.
whyWrong.B: The passage explains exactly why the gum behaves as it does, so nothing about it is mysterious.
whyWrong.C: Rarity would concern how uncommon the material is, which the text does not address.

tips: When a blank is joined to a named weakness by "at once … and," it has to be a benefit of the very same property.

whyCorrect: The passage says nothing coloured is added and that only the vessel changes, yet the yellow becomes an olive. So the iron is not contributing a colour of its own — it is altering the colour the plant liquor already gives. "Modifying" names that role exactly.

whyWrong.B: "Decorative" would suggest the iron adds an ornament, but the iron changes the existing colour rather than adding anything visible.
whyWrong.C: "Temporary" implies the effect fades, and the olive shade is permanent enough to be sold under its own name.
whyWrong.D: "Accidental" contradicts the passage, which says a dyer who wants the darker shade deliberately changes the pot.

commonMistakes: Assuming the iron must add colour; the sentence "nothing has been added that carries a colour of its own" rules that out.

whyCorrect: The problem stated first is that the new sheet cannot bear its own weight. The step described — turning it face down onto a felt so it leaves the wire — solves precisely that: it gives the sheet a support so it can be handled and stacked for pressing. The blank names the purpose of that transfer.

whyWrong.A: Whiteness comes from the furnish and bleaching, and no whitening is described.
whyWrong.C: Opacity is set by the fibres and the beating, not by laying the sheet on a felt.
whyWrong.D: The press changes thickness only as a by-product; the couching step described exists to get the fragile sheet off the wire.

tips: When a sentence names "a step whose only purpose is," look back for the problem the step solves.

whyCorrect: The sentences before establish a problem: the bath must be exactly right, but carragheen strength varies with the weed and the boiling, and errors in either direction spoil the work. The underlined sentence, opening with "therefore," gives what marblers do about it — a trial drop watched before the first sheet. It is the practical answer to the variability.

whyWrong.A: The boiling is mentioned earlier only as a source of variation; the underlined sentence describes a test, not a recipe.
whyWrong.B: Only one thickener is named in the passage, so no contrast between two methods exists.
whyWrong.C: Nobody abandons carragheen — the sentence describes how marblers go on using it successfully.

tips: A sentence beginning "therefore" is a response to what precedes it; identify the problem first.

whyCorrect: The passage puts two counts side by side — 480 sheets to a ream and 500 to a printer's ream — then explains the extra sheets as an allowance for spoilage in the press, and closes by saying the difference reflects two trades measuring for different purposes. Two figures followed by an account of the gap is the shape of the text.

whyWrong.B: No meaning narrows over time; both counts are in use at the same period.
whyWrong.C: The last sentence denies there is a dispute — it calls the difference a matter of purpose, not disagreement.
whyWrong.D: The text names units but recommends none of them.

commonMistakes: Reading "stationers sold by one count and printers bought by the other" as a quarrel; the passage explicitly says it is not.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts the old headband, sewn over a cord laced into the boards and taking real strain, with the modern one, a woven strip glued on and "fastened to nothing." The closing sentence names the result: what survives is the appearance of a structural member. A load-bearing part has become decoration.

whyWrong.A: No reason involving the price of silk is given; the change is described as machine binding keeping the look and dropping the work.
whyWrong.C: The modern headband is attached to nothing, so the passage implies it is weaker, not stronger.
whyWrong.D: The text mentions readers hooking a finger over the head of a book only to explain the old headband's function, and issues no advice.

tips: The last sentence of a short passage often states the main idea outright — read it before choosing.

whyCorrect: The leather is washed all over with glaire, so the wash alone decides nothing. Heat from the tool sets the glaire, and the passage says it holds the gold "where the tool touched and nowhere else." The pattern is fixed by where the heated tool lands on a coating already present.

whyWrong.A: The passage explicitly denies this: the gold is not held by an adhesive spread beforehand but by one that does nothing until the tool arrives.
whyWrong.B: Rubbing with an oiled rag removes surplus leaf after the fact; it does not decide where gold stuck.
whyWrong.C: No pattern is cut into the leather — the tool itself carries the design.

tips: When a passage says "not X but Y," one of the distractors will almost always be X.

whyCorrect: Lehr says constancy comes from comparing regions rather than measuring one region alone. The viewing tube removes every neighbouring region, leaving only the patch. If constancy disappears exactly when the comparison is made impossible, the comparison is what was producing it.

whyWrong.A: Naming times measure speed of response, not whether the judgement itself stays constant across illuminations.
whyWrong.B: Three cone types describe how wavelength is encoded at the retina and are compatible with either mechanism.
whyWrong.C: A decline with age says constancy can weaken but not what produces it.

tips: To test a mechanism, look for the finding that removes it and shows the effect vanishing with it.

whyCorrect: Ivimey says the dyer's evidence was shaped to blame the yarn rather than the dyeing. Choice A is built for that: two pieces in one bath at one time, identical treatment, and only the piece woven from the supplied Bradford yarn clouded. Holding the dyeing constant leaves the yarn as the only difference.

whyWrong.B: Long experience is a claim to general competence, not evidence about which of two causes produced this fault.
whyWrong.C: The price of indigo bears on cost, not on why the cloth clouded.
whyWrong.D: A description of the vat's temperature defends his practice in general but does not separate the yarn from the dyeing.

tips: Evidence that shifts blame works by holding the suspected cause constant and letting only the other factor vary.

whyCorrect: Oyelaran claims iron comes first and fungi later. Choice A supplies both halves: iron sits at the centre of every spot examined, and spots appear even where the store is too dry for fungi to grow. Spots without fungal growth cannot have been caused by fungi.

whyWrong.B: Culturing fungi from foxed sheets is consistent with either account, since Oyelaran agrees fungi arrive afterwards.
whyWrong.C: A date-related pattern might be explained by changes in papermaking or in storage, and it identifies no cause.
whyWrong.D: More spots in a damp store is what the fungal explanation predicts, so it works against her argument rather than for it.

commonMistakes: Accepting evidence that both hypotheses predict; useful evidence must separate them.

whyCorrect: The passage identifies the green as azurite that has converted to malachite in damp, and notes the conversion covers the whole sky but has left the ultramarine robe alone. The colour we see is a chemical change in one particular pigment, so it tells us about the material and not about what the painter meant the sky to look like.

whyWrong.B: Nothing about the conversion depends on when each area was painted; the difference is which pigment was used.
whyWrong.C: One robe in ultramarine says nothing about period-wide preferences for painting skies.
whyWrong.D: Cleaning is never mentioned, and a damp-driven chemical change is not evidence of it.

tips: When one area has altered and another has not, ask what differs between them — here the pigment, not the timing.

whyCorrect: Both mills can obtain recovered fibre; what separates them is that a carton does not have to survive folding while a paper that is folded and unfolded does, and short stiff recycled fibres bond poorly. The blank is set against "the fibre available to them," so it must name the demand each product places on the sheet.

whyWrong.A: Machinery age is never mentioned, and the passage attributes the limit to what the paper must withstand.
whyWrong.B: Price plays no part in the passage; the constraint described is physical, not commercial.
whyWrong.D: Collection quantity is another form of "fibre available," which the sentence explicitly sets aside.

tips: A blank following "less in X than in" must be genuinely different from X — check that the option is not a restatement of it.

whyCorrect: "A single scrap of coloured cloth left among the white will show in every sheet of the post" is a complete sentence, and "the sorters were the best paid women in the mill" is another. No conjunction joins them, so a semicolon is the correct mark.

whyWrong.A: With nothing between them the two sentences fuse, and "the post the sorters" reads as one confused noun phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon can introduce the second clause, but adding "and" after it gives two connectors doing one job.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

tips: Cover everything before the blank and check whether what follows is a full sentence; here it is, which rules out a comma.

whyCorrect: The subject is "the long fibres of the paper mulberry" and the verb is "make." Between them sits the nonessential phrase "beaten only enough to part them from one another," already opened by a comma, so it must be closed by one before the verb.

whyWrong.B: Without the closing comma the interrupting phrase runs into the verb and the sentence loses the pairing the first comma set up.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon must separate two independent clauses, but the verb "make" belongs to the subject before the interruption.
whyWrong.D: A colon would cut the subject off from its own verb, which no punctuation is allowed to do.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that a comma opening an interrupter obliges you to close it, even when the closing point falls just before the verb.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence announcing "three faults," and what follows is the list of those three. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces a list.

whyWrong.A: A comma here reads as though "a size too thin" continued the first clause, and it cannot introduce a list after a complete sentence.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the list runs straight into "touched it," so the reader cannot see the list beginning.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "a size too thin, a paper that has not been prepared, and a hand that hesitates" is a list of noun phrases.

tips: A sentence that promises a number of items — "three faults" — is nearly always followed by a colon and the items.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "Because the tone of a finished sheet is settled long before it reaches the vat," a dependent clause. An introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma before the main clause "the mill sorts its white rags…" begins.

whyWrong.B: Without the comma, "the vat the mill" runs together and the boundary between the clauses disappears.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and a because-clause cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.D: A colon must follow a complete sentence, which the opening clause is not.

tips: Whenever a sentence starts with because, although, when or since, expect a comma where the main clause starts.

whyCorrect: The subject of the clause is each, which is singular, so the possessive that follows must be singular too. "Its recipe" also matches the earlier "its yellow" in the same sentence.

whyWrong.A: "There" is not a possessive at all; it cannot show that the recipe belongs to anything.
whyWrong.C: "Their" is plural and would need a plural antecedent, but "each" is singular.
whyWrong.D: "It's" is the contraction of it is, giving the nonsensical "guarded it is recipe."

tips: Each, either, neither, every and any one are singular however many things they range over.

whyCorrect: The sentence fixes a past reference point — 1807, when the machine was fitted — and describes an activity that ran for ninety years up to that point. An action continuing up to a moment in the past takes the past perfect progressive, had been making.

whyWrong.B: "Have been making" runs up to the present, but the reference point is 1807.
whyWrong.C: "Are making" is present progressive and cannot describe ninety years ending in 1807.
whyWrong.D: "Make" is a simple present and gives no sense of a stretch of time completed before the machine arrived.

tips: "By the time" plus a past event is the classic signal for the past perfect.

whyCorrect: The sentence is inverted: the opening phrase "On the shelf above the muller" is a place, not the subject. The subject is "the four stoppered bottles of oil," which is plural, so the verb is stand.

whyWrong.A: "Has stood" is singular and also shifts to the present perfect, while the sentence describes a standing arrangement.
whyWrong.B: "Is standing" is singular and would agree with "shelf" or "muller," neither of which is the subject.
whyWrong.D: "Stands" is the singular form and cannot take a plural subject.

commonMistakes: Letting the first noun in the sentence set the verb; in an inverted sentence the subject comes after the verb.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim: some pigments react badly with what is around them. The second names a specific pigment, orpiment, and the specific damage it causes to the copper and lead colours next to it. A general claim followed by a named case takes an illustrative transition.

whyWrong.A: "Instead" would replace the first statement with an alternative, but the second sentence supports it.
whyWrong.C: "However" signals opposition, and the orpiment case confirms the warning rather than qualifying it.
whyWrong.D: "Therefore" would make the chemistry of orpiment a consequence of the general claim, when it is an instance of it.

tips: Naming a particular substance right after a general statement about substances is the signature of "for instance."

whyCorrect: The middle sentence sets up the stakes: the boil is a balance, and an hour too long ruins the paper months later. The last sentence reports what followed from those stakes — the foreman kept the timing to himself. Consequence of a stated risk calls for a result transition.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" would mean the secrecy held in spite of the risk, but the risk is exactly why it was kept secret.
whyWrong.B: "Similarly" claims a parallel case, and the last sentence is an outcome rather than a second example.
whyWrong.C: "In particular" narrows to a specific instance of something just described, and the foreman's practice is not an instance of the boiling damage.

tips: If the last sentence describes what someone did about the situation, the link is cause and effect.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences pile up advantages — needs no processing beyond grinding, costs next to nothing, covers well, does not fade. The third gives the outcome you would expect from that list: it is both the oldest identifiable pigment and still on sale. The transition should mark the outcome as the natural consequence.

whyWrong.A: "By contrast" needs an opposition, and the third sentence agrees with the first two.
whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" would mean the survival happened despite the advantages, which reverses the logic.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would make the third sentence an example of ochre's cheapness or permanence, but it is a conclusion drawn from them.

commonMistakes: Treating "not surprisingly" as a filler; it is doing the same work as "therefore" while acknowledging the reader can see it coming.

whyCorrect: The goal is the change in order, so the sentence has to say what was done when. Choice C makes the link explicit: because the guillotine takes hundreds of sheets at a stroke, trimming moved from after binding to before sewing.

whyWrong.A: This gives the machine's date and capacity but never mentions the stage at which trimming happens.
whyWrong.B: This is about re-trimming an already ploughed book and says nothing about sequence in manufacture.
whyWrong.D: This describes the old tool's slowness, which is a reason for change but not a statement of the new order.

tips: When the goal names a change in order or sequence, the answer must contain a before-and-after.

whyCorrect: The goal asks what after-images suggest about how colour signals are handled, so the sentence must run from the observation to the inference. Choice D does: the opposite-colour pairing rules out an explanation from cone types alone, and points to later cells that respond to differences between cone signals, excited by one member of a pair and inhibited by the other.

whyWrong.A: This reports the phenomenon and stops; no inference about processing is drawn.
whyWrong.B: This mixes an anatomical fact with the conditions for seeing an after-image and never connects them.
whyWrong.C: This states the mechanism without the after-image evidence, so it does not say what after-images suggest.

tips: When a goal asks what evidence "suggests," the winning option contains both the evidence and the conclusion.

whyCorrect: The goal is why the bran and madder go in. Choice B gives the chain: they feed bacteria, the bacteria strip out the oxygen, and only in the absence of oxygen does the blue dissolve. That is the reason for the addition.

whyWrong.A: This says the bacteria consume them but stops before the effect on oxygen and solubility, so no purpose is given.
whyWrong.C: This lists the ingredients and adds a piece of terminology about dead vats, neither of which explains the purpose.
whyWrong.D: This is an inventory of the vat, and for an audience already familiar with dyeing it adds nothing.

commonMistakes: Answering "what happens" when the goal asks "why it is done"; the purpose needs the final effect included.

whyCorrect: The passage gives melanin a mechanical role, not just a visual one: it packs into the barbs, leaves them harder and stiffer, and black tips wear less than white ones on the same wing. Wear resistance at the part of the wing that takes the most abrasion is a protective function.

whyWrong.B: "Decorative" is exactly what the passage argues against with the phrase "does not merely colour the barbs."
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text ties the black tips to a time of year.
whyWrong.D: Every feather colour is inherited, so calling it inherited explains nothing about why black appears at the wingtip in particular.

tips: When a passage says a feature does not merely do X, the answer names the additional job it does.

whyCorrect: The sentence is about whether two pieces of cloth still look the same under a different light. "Agree" is being used of colours matching one another, so the sense needed is one of correspondence between two things.

whyWrong.A: "Cooperate" needs agents working together, and cloth does not act.
whyWrong.B: "Conclude" means to reach a decision or bring to an end, which does not fit two pieces of cloth.
whyWrong.D: "Consent" is giving permission, a sense that requires a person.

tips: When a human-sounding verb is applied to objects, choose the option that describes a relation rather than an action.

whyCorrect: The passage describes wool as carrying sites along the fibre that bond with an acid dye, and cotton as offering "almost nothing" of the kind, which forces cotton dyers to use dyes that lodge inside or form a bond. The blank names what the colour needs from the fibre — something to hold on to. "Grip" is that.

whyWrong.A: "Outlast" is about durability over time, and the contrast drawn is about attachment, not longevity.
whyWrong.B: "Repeat" makes no sense of a dye's relation to a fibre.
whyWrong.D: "Cover" concerns spreading over a surface, but the passage says both fibres can be coloured through — the issue is what the dye attaches to.

tips: The sentence says the fibres differ "less in how deeply they can be coloured," so rule out any option about depth or coverage.

whyCorrect: "Drying" ordinarily means losing a liquid by evaporation. The passage says the oil film gains weight, nothing evaporates, and the change is a chemical reaction that cannot be undone. The word therefore describes the process wrongly, which is what "misleading" says.

whyWrong.A: "Technical" would suggest the term is specialised but accurate, and the passage's point is that it misdescribes what happens.
whyWrong.B: "Generous" would imply the paint is being flattered; the objection is about accuracy, not praise.
whyWrong.D: "Premature" would mean the film is not dry yet, but the passage says it hardens fully — the objection is to the word, not the timing.

commonMistakes: Reading the passage as saying the paint takes a long time to dry; it says the change is not drying at all.

whyCorrect: The passage rules out a rule of thumb — there is no number of turns, and the right point varies with the mineral and the oil. What is left is the colourman lifting the muller, looking and deciding. Deciding by trained inspection rather than by a rule is judgement.

whyWrong.A: "Chance" would make the outcome random, but the colourman is looking and deciding deliberately.
whyWrong.C: "Tradition" implies a handed-down practice, and the passage stresses that it changes with each material.
whyWrong.D: "Arithmetic" is exactly what the passage denies: there is no number of turns that settles it.

tips: When a passage rejects a fixed rule and describes someone inspecting and choosing, the blank is judgement or something like it.

whyCorrect: The sentences before explain that a laid mould's ribs and wires make the pulp settle unevenly. The underlined sentence tells the reader how to see that unevenness — hold the sheet to a window and the ladder of light and dark lines appears. It turns the described difference into something the reader can check.

whyWrong.A: No reason for abandoning laid moulds is given anywhere; the passage only describes what each type leaves.
whyWrong.B: It corrects nothing; the correction of a possible misreading comes in the last sentence, which says nothing was printed.
whyWrong.C: Both mould types have already been introduced before the underlined sentence.

tips: An imperative sentence in an expository passage usually invites the reader to observe or test what has just been explained.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts scroll and codex purely in terms of what a reader can do — reaching a middle passage, holding two places at once, moving between them — and the final sentence removes capacity and ease of manufacture as explanations. That leaves the reader's use as the account of why the format took over.

whyWrong.A: Nothing about sewing, boards or binding technique is described.
whyWrong.B: No dates or period of transition are given.
whyWrong.D: The last sentence says the codex is no easier to make; it makes no claim about which was better made.

commonMistakes: Missing the last sentence, which is there to eliminate the rival explanations and leave only the reader's convenience.

whyCorrect: The final sentence states the limit exactly: the strip shows "only that they are several and in what proportion" and "nothing about what those components are." So the method counts and proportions the components without identifying them.

whyWrong.A: Lightfastness is never tested; the strip records travel distance, not fading.
whyWrong.B: Binding to cloth is a separate property, and the clinging described is to the paper strip, not to fabric.
whyWrong.D: The passage denies exactly this — the strip shows nothing about the components' identity.

tips: When a passage ends by naming what a method cannot do, the answer usually pairs the capability with that limit.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the reason: the ground rock is a dull grey powder because the stone is mostly colourless mineral with the blue scattered through it. The wax-and-resin process exists to separate that scattered blue from everything else, which is why further treatment is needed.

whyWrong.A: Nothing says the blue fades; the problem is that it is diluted by colourless material.
whyWrong.B: The wax and resin hold the useless material back rather than deepening any colour.
whyWrong.D: Fineness of grinding is not the obstacle — the powder is already ground and still grey.

tips: A "why was further treatment needed" question is answered by the defect stated before the treatment is described.

whyCorrect: Take the difference for each mill: Fenton 1,150 − 240 = 910, Hulme 780 − 190 = 590, Marlow 2,100 − 520 = 1,580, Rushton 410 − 95 = 315. Marlow's gap of 1,580 folds is the largest, so Marlow is the paper the sentence needs.

whyWrong.A: Rushton has the smallest gap of the four, 315 folds, and also the lowest figures in both columns.
whyWrong.B: This gives only the along-grain figure for Fenton, so no difference can be computed, and Fenton's gap of 910 is smaller than Marlow's anyway.
whyWrong.C: This gives only Hulme's across-grain figure, and Hulme's gap of 590 is the second smallest.

commonMistakes: Picking the row with the biggest single number instead of subtracting the two columns.

whyCorrect: Cannon says the notebook exists to trace a bad sheet to the man who made it. Choice D states that purpose outright: each post is chalked with the vatman's own mark before pressing "so that a bad sheet may be carried back to him that made it." It records identity for accountability, not method.

whyWrong.A: Boiling times for different sorts of rag are exactly the record of how the paper was made that Cannon says the book is not for.
whyWrong.B: The price and wear of felts is a purchasing note and identifies no workman.
whyWrong.C: Hirings and a discharge are staff numbers; they do not link any sheet to any maker.

tips: When a claim is about someone's purpose, look for the quotation that contains a "so that" or its equivalent.

whyCorrect: Halloran's proposal is that comb spacing is a workshop fingerprint that survives in the sheet. Choice C tests it the right way: two workshops working to the same named pattern — so pattern alone cannot separate them — nonetheless differ consistently in line spacing. Consistency within a workshop and difference between workshops is what an attribution tool needs.

whyWrong.A: Who made the combs might explain why spacings differ, but it is not evidence that the spacing shows in the sheets or that it is consistent.
whyWrong.B: Shared pattern names across countries is the problem Halloran is trying to solve, not evidence that her method works.
whyWrong.D: A shared colour range is a different attribution criterion and says nothing about comb spacing.

tips: Evidence for an identification method must show it separating cases that the old method could not.

whyCorrect: Starlings have a fourth cone type sensitive in the ultraviolet, and the sex-specific markings are ultraviolet ones invisible to us. A human sorting by plumage alone is working without that channel, so the difference between males and females goes unnoticed by the observer while remaining plain to the birds.

whyWrong.B: The passage limits the failure to plumage seen by a human eye; other means, such as behaviour or examination, are not ruled out.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the comparison — the starling has the extra receptor and therefore the advantage.
whyWrong.D: The passage states that these feathers reflect strongly in the ultraviolet, so that conclusion would be wrong.

commonMistakes: Overstating the inference into a claim that the sexes cannot be told apart at all; only the plumage route is blocked.

whyCorrect: The passage supplies a mechanism and a controlled comparison: vellum cockles as it takes up and gives back moisture, clasped volumes still open flat after five centuries, and volumes whose clasps were removed have cockled leaves. The clasp is what supplies the pressure that keeps the leaves flat.

whyWrong.A: The passage attributes the movement to vellum leaves, not to the boards, and it is the leaves that cockle when the clasp goes.
whyWrong.C: Security is never mentioned; the contrast in the passage is between flat leaves and cockled ones.
whyWrong.D: The stripped volumes cockle, so the loss makes a plain practical difference.

tips: When a passage gives you a with-and-without comparison, the answer is the function that the "without" case loses.

whyCorrect: "A colourman's apprentice was bound to the trade for seven years" and "he could not set up on his own account until the whole term had been served" are both independent clauses, joined here by the coordinating conjunction and. That construction takes a comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: Omitting the comma leaves two independent clauses joined by "and" alone, which the convention does not allow.
whyWrong.B: A comma with no conjunction between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon already joins the clauses by itself, and the extra comma after "and" cuts the second subject off from its clause.

tips: The presence of "he" in the blank is the clue — it makes the second half a full clause with its own subject.

whyCorrect: "Mauveine" is a nonessential appositive naming the dye, dropped into the middle of the sentence between the subject and its verb "was found." A nonessential element takes a comma on both sides.

whyWrong.B: With only the closing comma the appositive is unbalanced, and "Perkin's fortune mauveine" reads as a single garbled noun phrase.
whyWrong.C: With only the opening comma the appositive never closes, so "mauveine was found" reads as the start of a new clause.
whyWrong.D: A colon has to follow a complete sentence, and "The dye that made Perkin's fortune" has no verb of its own yet.

tips: An appositive in mid-sentence needs matching marks; if you use a comma to open it, use a comma to close it.

whyCorrect: The day book lists three jobs, and each item already contains its own internal comma — half calf, for the cathedral library; cloth, for a school; vellum, for a private buyer. When list items contain commas, the items are separated by semicolons, and the sentence already uses one after "library."

whyWrong.A: With no mark before "and one," the third item runs into the second and the list loses its structure.
whyWrong.B: A colon has already done its work introducing the list; it cannot also separate items within it.
whyWrong.D: A comma cannot separate items that contain commas of their own — that is exactly the situation semicolons exist for.

tips: Look at how the earlier items in a list are punctuated; the blank should match.

whyCorrect: "Sheets are hung to dry in spurs of four or five over ropes strung the length of the drying loft" is a complete sentence, and "the loft is boarded on all sides with slats the miller can open and shut …" is another. With no coordinating conjunction, a semicolon makes the join.

whyWrong.A: A colon followed by "and" pairs two connectors, and the second clause adds a new fact rather than explaining the first.
whyWrong.C: A comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no mark at all the two clauses fuse into a run-on.

tips: Watch for a repeated noun across the join — "drying loft" then "the loft" — which usually marks the start of a new independent clause.
